notes.front: What is the Brayton cycle?
notes.back: The thermodynamic cycle a gas turbine engine uses to produce thrust: a variable-volume, constant-pressure cycle of events.
notes.explanation: Because its pressure stays nearly constant, it is commonly called the constant-pressure cycle.
notes.example: Like the four-stroke cycle of a piston engine, but each event has its own section of the engine and none of them ever pauses.
notes.evidence: The Brayton cycle is the name given to the thermodynamic cycle of a gas turbine engine to produce thrust. This is a variable volume constant-pressure cycle of events and is commonly called the constant-pressure cycle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: In powerplant terms, what is thrust?
notes.back: The aerodynamic force produced as a propeller or turbojet engine forces a mass of air rearward, behind the aircraft.
notes.explanation: A propeller accelerates a large mass of air by a small amount; a turbojet accelerates a smaller mass by a much larger amount.
notes.example: Like the push a garden hose gives your hands as water leaves the nozzle, but from air thrown rearward.
notes.evidence: Thrust. The aerodynamic force produced by a propeller or turbojet engine as it forces a mass of air to the rear, behind the aircraft. A propeller produces its thrust by accelerating a large mass of air by a relatively small amount.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Thrust”, p. G-28

notes.front: What is ram recovery in a gas turbine engine?
notes.back: Regaining thrust from ram pressure: forward speed raises inlet pressure above atmospheric, increasing mass airflow and gas velocity.
notes.explanation: Ram pressure is the rise above outside atmospheric pressure at the inlet caused by the aircraft moving forward.
notes.example: Like feeling air pile up against a hand held out of a moving car window, but at the engine inlet.
notes.evidence: A rise in pressure above existing outside atmospheric pressure at the engine inlet, as a result of the forward velocity of an aircraft, is referred to as ram pressure. Since any ram effect causes an increase in compressor entrance pressure over atmospheric, the resulting pressure rise causes an increase in the mass airflow and gas velocity
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Ram Recovery”, p. 1-60

notes.front: What is a turbojet engine?
notes.back: A gas turbine engine that produces thrust by accelerating the air flowing through it, with a minimum of energy taken by the turbine.
notes.explanation: Most of the energy goes into an exhaust velocity much greater than the inlet velocity.
notes.example: Like a hose nozzle that speeds a small stream to high velocity, rather than a fan moving a big, slow stream.
notes.evidence: Turbojet engine. A gas turbine engine that produces thrust by accelerating the air flowing through it. A minimum of energy is extracted by the turbine, with the majority used to produce an exhaust velocity much greater than the inlet velocity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Turbojet engine”, p. G-29

notes.front: What is a turboprop engine?
notes.back: A combination of a gas turbine engine, a reduction gearbox and a propeller.
notes.explanation: Its gas generator (compressor, combustion chambers, turbine and exhaust nozzle) works as in any other gas turbine engine.
notes.example: Like a piston-engined aircraft's propeller installation, but the propeller is turned by a turbine through reduction gears.
notes.evidence: The turbopropeller (turboprop) engine is a combination of a gas turbine engine, reduction gear box, and a propeller. [Figure 1-78] Turboprops are basically gas turbine engines that have a compressor, combustion chamber(s), turbine, and an exhaust nozzle (gas generator)
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboprop Engines”, p. 1-54

notes.front: What is a turbofan engine?
notes.back: In principle a turboprop whose propeller is replaced by a duct-enclosed axial-flow fan.
notes.explanation: The fan may be part of the first-stage compressor blades or a separate set of fan blades.
notes.example: Like a turboprop whose propeller has been shrunk, given many more blades and wrapped in a duct.
notes.evidence: The turbofan gas turbine engine is, in principle, the same as a turboprop, except that the propeller is replaced by a ductenclosed axial-flow fan. [Figure 1-80] The fan can be a part of the first-stage compressor blades or can be mounted as a separate set of fan blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbofan Engines”, p. 1-55

notes.front: What is the bypass ratio of a turbofan engine?
notes.back: The ratio of airflow (lb/sec) from the fan bypass to the airflow through the engine's core.
notes.explanation: The air driven by the fan generally does not pass through the internal working core, so the two flows are measured separately.
notes.example: Like a crowd where six people walk round a building for every one who walks through it: a 6:1 ratio.
notes.evidence: the air generally driven by the fan does not pass through the internal working core of the engine. The amount of air flow in lb/sec from the fan bypass to the core flow of the engine is the bypass ratio.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: What is a turboshaft engine?
notes.back: A gas turbine engine that delivers power through a shaft to operate something other than a propeller.
notes.explanation: The output shaft may be coupled directly to the engine turbine or driven by a turbine of its own in the exhaust stream.
notes.example: Like a turboprop, but the shaft turns a helicopter's rotor transmission instead of a propeller.
notes.evidence: A gas-turbine engine that delivers power through a shaft to operate something other than a propeller is referred to as a turboshaft engine. [Figure 1-79] The output shaft may be coupled directly to the engine turbine, or the shaft may be driven by a turbine of its own (free turbine) located in the exhaust stream.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboshaft Engines”, p. 1-55

notes.front: What is a free turbine?
notes.back: A turbine stage on a shaft independent of the shaft used to drive the compressor.
notes.explanation: Free turbines drive the propeller reduction gear in turboprops and the rotor transmission in helicopters.
notes.example: Like a windmill placed in a fan's blast: it spins in the airflow, but no shaft joins it to the fan.
notes.evidence: Free-turbine engine. A gas turbine engine with a turbine stage on a shaft independent of the shaft used to drive the compressor. Free turbines are used to drive the propeller reduction gear in a turboprop engine and the rotor transmission in a helicopter.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Free-turbine engine”, p. G-13

notes.front: What is the air entrance of a gas turbine engine designed to do?
notes.back: Conduct incoming air to the compressor with minimum energy loss from drag or ram pressure loss, free of turbulence.
notes.explanation: Turbulence-free flow into the compressor is what achieves maximum operating efficiency.
notes.example: Like a smooth, flared funnel on a vacuum hose, shaped so the air arrives without swirling.
notes.evidence: The air entrance is designed to conduct incoming air to the compressor with a minimum energy loss resulting from drag or ram pressure loss; that is, the flow of air into the compressor should be free of turbulence to achieve maximum operating efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Air Entrance”, p. 1-37

notes.front: On a turbofan, what is the accessory gearbox?
notes.back: The gearbox, usually on the bottom of the engine, on which the driven accessories are mounted.
notes.explanation: Its location varies; most turboprops and turboshafts mount their accessory cases at the back of the engine instead.
notes.example: Like a car engine's belt-driven alternator and pumps, but driven through gears and mounted under the engine.
notes.evidence: Driven accessories on turbofans are usually mounted on the accessory gear box, which is on the bottom of the engine. The location of the accessory gear box varies somewhat, but most turboprops and turboshafts have the accessory cases mounted to the back section of the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Accessory Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: What is a centrifugal-flow compressor?
notes.back: A compressor with a vaned, plate-like impeller that takes air in at its eye and slings it outward into a diffuser.
notes.explanation: In the diffuser the air slows down and its pressure rises.
notes.example: Like a salad spinner flinging water to its rim, but flinging air into a ring of widening passages.
notes.evidence: Centrifugal compressor. A type of compressor that uses a vaned plate like impeller. Air is taken into the center, or eye, of the impeller and slung outward by centrifugal force into a diffuser where its velocity is decreased and its pressure increased.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Centrifugal compressor”, p. G-6

notes.front: What is an axial-flow compressor?
notes.back: A compressor in which air passes in an essentially straight line, parallel to its axis, through stages of rotating blades and stationary vanes.
notes.explanation: Each stage of rotating compressor blades sits between stages of stationary stator vanes.
notes.example: Like a row of desk fans lined up in a tube, each passing air to the next, with fixed vanes between them.
notes.evidence: Axial-flow compressor. A type of compressor used in gas turbine engines. Air passes through the compressor in essentially a straight line, parallel to the axis of the compressor. The compressor is made of a number of stages of rotating compressor blades between stages of stationary stator vanes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Axial-flow compressor”, p. G-3

notes.front: What is the compressor pressure ratio?
notes.back: Compressor outlet (discharge) pressure divided by its inlet pressure.
notes.explanation: Proper inlet design raises this ratio, which is how the inlet contributes to aircraft performance.
notes.example: Like a tyre pump taking air in at 15 psi and delivering it at 150 psi: a 10:1 ratio.
notes.evidence: Proper inlet design contributes materially to aircraft performance by increasing the ratio of compressor discharge pressure to duct inlet pressure. This is also referred to as the compressor pressure ratio. This ratio is the outlet pressure divided by the inlet pressure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Air Entrance”, p. 1-37

notes.front: In a gas turbine engine, what is a spool?
notes.back: A compressor together with the shaft and turbines that drive that compressor.
notes.explanation: A two-shaft turbofan has two sets of compressors, each with the turbines that drive it, so it has two spools.
notes.example: Like two cotton reels on one axle, each free to turn at its own speed.
notes.evidence: This means that there are two sets of compressors and turbines that drive them. These two-shafted engines use two spools (a spool is a compressor and a shaft and turbines that drive that compressor).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: What are inlet guide vanes in a gas turbine compressor?
notes.back: Stator vanes in front of the first compression stage that deflect entering air in the correct direction; fixed or variable.
notes.explanation: Where their angle varies, it is controlled hydraulically by fuel from the fuel control.
notes.example: Like fixed louvres at the mouth of a duct, but aiming the air at the first row of rotor blades.
notes.evidence: Inlet guide vanes. A set of stator vanes in front of the first stage of compression in a gas turbine engine. The inlet guide vanes deflect the air entering the compressor in the correct direction for optimum operation. Inlet guide vanes may be fixed, or their angle may be controlled hydraulically by fuel from the fuel control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Inlet guide vanes”, p. G-15

notes.front: What are axial compressor rotor blades usually made of, and how are they attached?
notes.back: Usually stainless steel, with titanium in the latter stages; commonly fitted into the discs by bulb-type or fir-tree roots.
notes.explanation: After fitting into the disc, the blades are locked in place by differing methods.
notes.example: Like the blades of a ceiling fan, but many rows of small aerofoils slotted into a spinning disc.
notes.evidence: The rotor blades are usually made of stainless steel with the latter stages being made of titanium. The design of blade attachment to the rotor disc rims varies, but they are commonly fitted into discs by either bulb-type or fir-tree methods. [Figure 1-49] The blades are then locked into place by differing methods.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-41

notes.front: What does the diffuser of a gas turbine engine do?
notes.back: It turns high-velocity compressor discharge air into higher pressure at a slower velocity.
notes.explanation: Slower air entering the flame area lets the flame of combustion burn continuously.
notes.example: Like a river widening into a lake: the water slows down and its pressure energy rises.
notes.evidence: It has the all-important function of reducing high-velocity compressor discharge air to increased pressure at a slower velocity. This prepares the air for entry into the flame burning area of the combustion section at a lower velocity so that the flame of combustion can burn continuously.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Diffuser”, p. 1-43

notes.front: What does the combustion section of a gas turbine engine do?
notes.back: It houses the combustion process, which raises the temperature of the air passing through and releases the energy in the air-fuel mixture.
notes.explanation: Most of that energy is then needed at the turbine stages to drive the compressor.
notes.example: Like a gas cooker's burner, but burning continuously in a stream of compressed air.
notes.evidence: The combustion section houses the combustion process, which raises the temperature of the air passing through the engine. This process releases energy contained in the airfuel mixture. The major part of this energy is required at the turbine or turbine stages to drive the compressor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-43

notes.front: What is a can-type combustion chamber?
notes.back: Separate chambers, each an outer case around a perforated, heat-resistant stainless steel liner; typical of turboshafts and APUs.
notes.explanation: The outer case is removed when the liner needs replacing.
notes.example: Like a ring of separate tin cans round the engine shaft, each with its own burner.
notes.evidence: The can-type combustion chamber is typical of the type used on turboshaft and APUs. [Figure 1-52] Each of the can-type combustion chambers consists of an outer case or housing, within which there is a perforated stainless steel (highly heat resistant) combustion chamber liner or inner liner. [Figure 1-53] The outer case is removed to facilitate liner replacement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-43

notes.front: What is an annular combustion chamber?
notes.back: A housing and a liner, the liner being one undivided circular shroud all the way round the turbine shaft housing.
notes.explanation: Its basic components, a housing and a liner, are the same as in the can type; only the liner is undivided.
notes.example: Like one ring-shaped burner in place of a ring of separate cans.
notes.evidence: The basic components of an annular combustion chamber are a housing and a liner, as in the can type. The liner consists of an undivided circular shroud extending all the way around the outside of the turbine shaft housing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: What is a can-annular combustion chamber?
notes.back: Individual cans, where fuel is sprayed and ignited, mounted on an annular duct that directs the hot gases uniformly into the turbine.
notes.explanation: The glossary places it in some large turbojet and turbofan engines.
notes.example: Like several separate burners feeding one shared ring-shaped chimney.
notes.evidence: Can-annular combustor. A type of combustor used in some large turbojet and turbofan engines. It consists of individual cans into which fuel is sprayed and ignited. These cans mount on an annular duct which collects the hot gases and directs them uniformly into the turbine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Can-annular combustor”, p. G-5

notes.front: What does the turbine section of a gas turbine engine do?
notes.back: It turns part of the exhaust gases' velocity energy into mechanical energy to drive the gas generator compressor and accessories.
notes.explanation: The gas generator turbine absorbs roughly 60 to 70 percent of the total pressure energy in the exhaust gases.
notes.example: Like a windmill in the exhaust stream whose shaft turns the compressor at the front.
notes.evidence: The turbine transforms a portion of the kinetic (velocity) energy of the exhaust gases into mechanical energy to drive the gas generator compressor and accessories. The sole purpose of the gas generator turbine is to absorb approximately 60 to 70 percent of the total pressure energy from the exhaust gases.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: What is the turbine nozzle?
notes.back: Another name for the turbine inlet guide vanes: stator vanes just ahead of the first-stage turbine.
notes.explanation: They divert the hot gases in the proper direction to enter the turbine and form convergent ducts that increase gas velocity.
notes.example: Like the nozzle on a hose aimed at a water wheel's paddles.
notes.evidence: Turbine inlet guide vanes. A series of stator vanes immediately ahead of the first-stage turbine. The function of the inlet guide vanes is to divert the hot gases in the proper direction to enter the turbine, and to provide a series of convergent ducts which increase the velocity of the gases. Turbine nozzle. Another name for turbine inlet guide vanes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Turbine inlet guide vanes”, p. G-29

notes.front: What is a fir-tree root?
notes.back: A blade root of fir-tree design fitting a matching groove in the disc; the most satisfactory way of attaching turbine blades.
notes.explanation: Turbine blades are attached in several ways, some like compressor blades, and the handbook rates the fir-tree design best.
notes.example: Like a dovetail joint in woodwork, but with several stepped lobes holding the blade in the disc.
notes.evidence: There are various ways of attaching turbine blades, some similar to compressor blade attachment. The most satisfactory method utilizes the fir-tree design.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-49

notes.front: What are shrouded turbine blades?
notes.back: Turbine blades whose tips, in effect, form a band around the outer perimeter of the turbine wheel.
notes.explanation: The band improves efficiency and vibration and permits lighter stages, but limits turbine speed and needs more blades.
notes.example: Like a bicycle wheel's rim tying the spoke ends together, but round the tips of turbine blades.
notes.evidence: The shrouded turbine blades, in effect, form a band around the outer perimeter of the turbine wheel. This improves efficiency and vibration characteristics and permits lighter stage weights. On the other hand, it limits turbine speed and requires more blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-50

notes.front: What does the exhaust cone do?
notes.back: It collects the gases leaving the turbine and gradually converts them into a solid flow, slightly slowing them and raising their pressure.
notes.explanation: The slowing comes from the diverging passage between the outer duct and the inner cone.
notes.example: Like the tapering tail of a teardrop, filling the space behind the turbine hub.
notes.evidence: The exhaust cone collects the exhaust gases discharged from the turbine section and gradually converts them into a solid flow of gases. In performing this, the velocity of the gases is decreased slightly and the pressure increased. This is due to the diverging passage between the outer duct and the inner cone
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Exhaust Section”, p. 1-51

notes.front: What is a labyrinth seal?
notes.back: A seal round the main-shaft bearings: rotating blades that almost touch the seal land, with a little air flowing between them.
notes.explanation: That small flow of air between seal and land is what stops oil flowing past the seal.
notes.example: Like a comb held almost against a surface, with air leaking through its teeth to hold oil back.
notes.evidence: Labyrinth seal. A type of air and/or seal used around the main –shaft bearings in a gas turbine engine. The seal consists of a series of rotating blades that almost contact the seal land. A small amount of air flows between the seal and the land to prevent oil flowing past the seal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Labyrinth seal”, p. G-16

notes.front: What is the flat rating of a turbine engine?
notes.back: The thrust performance the manufacturer guarantees for a new engine under specific conditions, such as takeoff, maximum continuous climb and cruise.
notes.explanation: It is a guarantee for a new engine, tied to named power settings.
notes.example: Like a car maker's guaranteed acceleration figure for a new car under stated test conditions.
notes.evidence: The flat rating of a turbine engine is the thrust performance that is guaranteed by the manufacturer for a new engine under specific operating conditions, such as takeoff, maximum continuous climb, and cruise power settings.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Ratings”, p. 10-54

notes.front: What is blending of blades?
notes.back: Repairing a damaged compressor or turbine blade by filing the damage into a shallow depression with generous radii, then stoning it smooth.
notes.explanation: The stoning removes the file marks so the repaired area matches the surface of the rest of the blade.
notes.example: Like sanding a chip in a table edge into a smooth, shallow scoop instead of filling it.
notes.evidence: Blending. A method of repairing damaged compressor and turbine blades. The damage is removed and the area is cleaned out with a fine file to form a shallow depression with generous radii. The file marks are then removed with a fine abrasive stone so the surface of the repaired area will match the surface of the rest of the blade.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Blending”, p. G-4

notes.front: What is engine trim (trimming the engine)?
notes.back: Adjusting a turbine engine fuel control's idle rpm and maximum speed after the control is fitted.
notes.explanation: Field repair of the fuel control is limited to replacing it and making these adjustments.
notes.example: Like setting a new carburettor's idle and full-power stops after fitting it, but against the manufacturer's charts.
notes.evidence: The only repairs permitted in the field are the replacement of the control and adjustments afterwards. These adjustments are limited to the idle rpm and the maximum speed adjustment, commonly called trimming the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-40

notes.front: What is turbine engine condition monitoring?
notes.back: A program that tracks certain engine parameters daily and watches for trend shifts, to judge the engine's health in service.
notes.explanation: It is also called trend analysis performance monitoring.
notes.example: Like weighing yourself daily and noticing a steady drift rather than one odd reading.
notes.evidence: Many turbine engines are monitored by an engine condition program that helps determine the health of the engine in service. This can also be called trend analysis performance monitoring, but it consists mainly of monitoring certain engine parameters daily and watching for trend shifts or changes in the engine parameters.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Turbine Engine Condition Monitoring Programs”, p. 8-2

notes.front: What is a compressor stall?
notes.back: A condition in an axial-flow compressor where the angle of attack of one or more blades is excessive, disrupting smooth airflow.
notes.explanation: It is defined at blade level, by the angle of attack of individual blades.
notes.example: Like a wing stalling at too high an angle of attack, but on compressor blades.
notes.evidence: Compressor stall. A condition in a turbine engine axial-flow compressor in which the angle of attack of one or more blades is excessive and the smooth airflow through the compressor is disrupted.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Compressor stall”, p. G-7

notes.front: What is compressor bleed air?
notes.back: Air tapped off a turbine engine's compressor.
notes.explanation: It anti-ices the inlet ducts, cools the turbine inlet guide vanes and first-stage blades, and serves some airframe functions.
notes.example: Like opening a side valve on a compressed-air line to run a tool.
notes.evidence: Compressor bleed air. Air that is tapped off from a turbine engine compressor. Compressor bleed air is used for antiicing the inlet ducts and for cooling the turbine inlet guide vanes and first stage turbine blades. Bleed air is also used for certain airframe functions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Compressor bleed air”, p. G-7

notes.front: What is a quick engine change assembly (QECA)?
notes.back: A powerplant with its necessary accessories already installed; also called the engine power package.
notes.explanation: Commercial operators use it for the most efficient and expeditious replacement of engines.
notes.example: Like swapping a complete, pre-assembled engine and gearbox rather than building one up in the car.
notes.evidence: Commercial operators, whose maintenance operations require the most efficient and expeditious replacement of aircraft engines, usually rely on a system that utilizes the quick-engine-change assembly (QECA), also sometimes referred to as the engine power package.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Preparation of Engines for Installation”, p. 8-3

notes.front: What is a full authority digital electronic control (FADEC)?
notes.back: Full authority digital electronic control: electronic control of fuel flow, developed for most new turbine engines.
notes.explanation: A true system has no hydromechanical fuel control backup, so the electronics have full authority.
notes.example: Like a car's engine-management computer, but with no mechanical fallback at all.
notes.evidence: A full authority digital electronic control (FADEC) has been developed to control fuel flow on most new turbine engine models. A true FADEC system has no hydromechanical fuel control backup system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “FADEC Fuel Control Systems”, p. 2-36

notes.front: In a piston engine all four events share one chamber. How does a gas turbine engine differ?
notes.back: Separate sections are devoted to each function, and all functions are performed simultaneously without interruption.
notes.explanation: In a reciprocating engine each event must have exclusive use of the chamber in turn.
notes.evidence: Consequently, each must have exclusive occupancy of the chamber during its respective part of the combustion cycle. A significant feature of the gas turbine engine is that separate sections are devoted to each function, and all functions are performed simultaneously without interruption.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: An apprentice lists the sections air meets in a typical gas turbine engine. Which order is right?
notes.back: D: Inlet, compressor, combustion, turbine, exhaust
notes.explanation: The handbook lists the sections in this order, with the accessory section and supporting systems besides.
notes.choices:
A) Inlet, combustion, compressor, turbine, exhaust
B) Inlet, compressor, turbine, combustion, exhaust
C) Compressor, inlet, combustion, exhaust, turbine
D) Inlet, compressor, combustion, turbine, exhaust
notes.choicesExplained: A puts combustion before compression. B burns the air after the turbine. C starts behind the inlet and ends at the turbine.
notes.evidence: A typical gas turbine engine consists of: 1. An air inlet, 2. Compressor section, 3. Combustion section, 4. Turbine section, 5. Exhaust section, 6. Accessory section
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: The four continuous events of the Brayton cycle are intake, compression, {{c1::expansion (which includes power)}} and exhaust.
notes.back: Expansion, which includes power.
notes.explanation: The four events are continuous and constant, not taken in turn as in a piston engine.
notes.evidence: The four continuous and constant events are intake, compression, expansion (includes power), and exhaust.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: A student says a gas turbine burns its fuel at constant volume, like a piston engine at top dead centre. Which reply is right?
notes.back: B: Wrong: pressure stays nearly constant while volume grows
notes.explanation: The Brayton cycle is a variable-volume, constant-pressure cycle.
notes.choices:
A) Correct: the Brayton cycle is a constant-volume cycle
B) Wrong: in the Brayton cycle pressure stays nearly constant while the volume grows
C) Wrong: pressure and volume both fall during combustion
D) Correct, but only on turbofans
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the cycle's defining feature. C contradicts the marked volume increase. D invents a difference between engine types.
notes.evidence: The pressure remains relatively constant, but a marked increase in volume takes place.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: Which law is the propulsive principle of a gas turbine engine based on?
notes.back: Newton's third law: the engine accelerates a mass of air (action) and so applies a force on the aircraft (reaction).
notes.explanation: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, so accelerating air rearward pushes the aircraft forward.
notes.evidence: The principle used by a gas turbine engine as it provides force to move an airplane is based on Newton's Third Law. This law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; therefore, if the engine accelerates a mass of air (action), it applies a force on the aircraft (reaction).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Engine Operating Principles”, p. 1-56

notes.front: Applying Bernoulli's principle, what do convergent and divergent ducts do to subsonic airflow?
notes.back: Convergent: velocity up, pressure down. Divergent: velocity down, pressure up.
notes.explanation: The handbook applies Bernoulli's principle to gas turbines through these two duct shapes.
notes.evidence: The convergent duct increases velocity and decreases pressure. The divergent duct decreases velocity and increases pressure. The convergent principle is usually used for the exhaust nozzle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: Air slows and gains pressure as it passes through one part of a gas turbine. Which duct principle is at work, and where?
notes.back: D: Divergent, in the compressor and diffuser
notes.explanation: Slowing air and raising its pressure is what a divergent duct does, and the compressor and diffuser use it.
notes.choices:
A) Convergent, in the exhaust nozzle
B) Divergent, in the turbine nozzle
C) Convergent, in the diffuser
D) Divergent, in the compressor and diffuser
notes.choicesExplained: A: a convergent duct speeds air up. B: the turbine nozzle forms convergent ducts. C: the diffuser is divergent, not convergent.
notes.evidence: The divergent principle is used in the compressor and diffuser where the air is slowing and pressurizing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: How does the way a turbofan makes thrust differ from the old pure turbojet?
notes.back: Turbofan: a relatively slower acceleration of a large quantity of air. Turbojet: greater acceleration of a smaller quantity.
notes.explanation: The turbojet's method was its main problem with fuel consumption and noise.
notes.evidence: The turbofan generates thrust by giving a relatively slower acceleration to a large quantity of air. The old pure turbojet engine achieves thrust by imparting greater acceleration to a smaller quantity of air. This was its main problem with fuel consumption and noise.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Engine Operating Principles”, p. 1-56

notes.front: What formula gives the thrust of a turbojet engine?
notes.back: Thrust = mass flow (lb/sec) × change in velocity (jet minus inlet) ÷ gravity (32.2 ft/sec²).
notes.explanation: The thrust equals the force needed to accelerate the air mass through the engine.
notes.evidence: V2 - V1 = change in velocity; difference between inlet velocity and jet velocity G = acceleration of gravity or 32.2 ft/sec2
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: An engine moves 64.4 lb of air per second, accelerating it from 500 ft/sec to 1,000 ft/sec. What thrust does it produce?
notes.choicesExplained: A uses a gravity of 16.1 instead of 32.2. B is the velocity change alone, without the mass flow ÷ gravity factor (64.4 ÷ 32.2 = 2). D multiplies mass flow by the velocity change but never divides by gravity (64.4 × 500).
notes.evidence: Ms = mass flow in lb/sec V1 = inlet velocity V2 = jet velocity (exhaust) V2 - V1 = change in velocity; difference between inlet velocity and jet velocity G = acceleration of gravity or 32.2 ft/sec2
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: By what two methods can the thrust of a gas turbine engine be increased?
notes.back: Increase the mass flow of air through the engine, or increase the gas velocity.
notes.explanation: Both terms appear in the thrust formula: mass flow and the change in velocity.
notes.evidence: Thrust of a gas turbine engine can be increased by two methods: increasing the mass flow of air through the engine or increasing the gas velocity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Thrust”, p. 1-58

notes.front: What are the three most important factors affecting gas turbine thermal efficiency?
notes.back: Turbine inlet temperature, compression ratio, and the component efficiencies of the compressor and turbine.
notes.explanation: Compressor inlet temperature and combustion efficiency also affect it, but less.
notes.evidence: The three most important factors affecting the thermal efficiency are turbine inlet temperature, compression ratio, and the component efficiencies of the compressor and turbine. Other factors that affect thermal efficiency are compressor inlet temperature and combustion efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Performance”, p. 1-59

notes.front: At constant altitude, rpm and airspeed, how does a fall in outside air temperature affect thrust, and why?
notes.back: Thrust improves rapidly: less energy per pound of air drives the compressor, and denser air raises mass flow.
notes.explanation: The compressor's energy need per pound of airflow varies directly with temperature, leaving more for thrust.
notes.evidence: This increase occurs partly because the energy required per pound of airflow to drive the compressor varies directly with the temperature, leaving more energy to develop thrust. In addition, the thrust output increases since the air at reduced temperature has an increased density.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Performance”, p. 1-59

notes.front: What is the net effect of increasing altitude on turbine engine thrust?
notes.back: Thrust falls: the drop in density more than offsets the benefit of colder air.
notes.explanation: Temperature lapses more slowly than pressure with altitude, so density decreases.
notes.evidence: Although the decreased temperature increases thrust, the effect of decreased density more than offsets the effect of the colder temperature. The net result of increased altitude is a reduction in the thrust output.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Performance”, p. 1-59

notes.front: The same engine is run at the same rpm, altitude and airspeed on a −10 °C morning and a 35 °C afternoon. When does it give more thrust?
notes.back: A: On the cold morning
notes.explanation: Thrust output improves rapidly as outside air temperature falls at constant altitude, rpm and airspeed.
notes.choices:
A) On the cold morning
B) On the hot afternoon
C) The same both times, since rpm is fixed
D) It cannot be told without humidity
notes.choicesExplained: B reverses the temperature effect. C ignores the change in air density. D: the handbook links thrust to outside air temperature at constant altitude, rpm and airspeed, and needs no humidity figure.
notes.evidence: Figure 1-84 shows that the thrust output improves rapidly with a reduction in outside air temperature (OAT) at constant altitude, rpm, and airspeed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Performance”, p. 1-59

notes.front: At a given throttle setting, how does thrust change as an aircraft accelerates from standstill?
notes.back: It decreases at first, soon stops decreasing, then increases again at higher speeds from ram recovery.
notes.explanation: Two opposing trends act as speed rises, and the result is their net effect.
notes.evidence: An engine's thrust output temporarily decreases as aircraft speed increases from static, but soon ceases to decrease. Moving toward higher speeds, thrust output begins to increase again due to the increased pressure of ram recovery.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Ram Recovery”, p. 1-60

notes.front: Why is the use of pure turbojet engines now very limited?
notes.back: They have problems with noise and fuel consumption in the speed range airliners fly (.8 Mach).
notes.explanation: Turbofans replaced them on almost all airliner-type aircraft for this reason.
notes.evidence: The turbojet engine has problems with noise and fuel consumption in the speed range that airliners fly (.8 Mach). Due to these problems, use of pure turbojet engines is very limited.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: About how much of a turbofan engine's thrust does its fan produce?
notes.back: About 80 percent.
notes.explanation: The fan, a large fan or set of fans at the front of the engine, is what the turbofan was developed to turn.
notes.evidence: It was developed to turn a large fan or set of fans at the front of the engine and produces about 80 percent of the thrust from the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: What is the main advantage of a turbofan converting more fuel energy into pressure?
notes.back: It produces additional thrust without increasing fuel flow, giving fuel economy and increased range.
notes.explanation: More energy as pressure gives a greater product of pressure times area.
notes.evidence: converted to pressure, a greater product of pressure times area can be achieved. One of the major advantages is turbofan production of this additional thrust without increasing fuel flow. The end result is fuel economy with the consequent increase in range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbofan Engines”, p. 1-56

notes.front: The turbofan is a compromise between which two engines' strengths?
notes.back: The turboprop's good operating efficiency and high thrust, and the turbojet's high speed, high altitude capability.
notes.explanation: This compromise makes turbofans the most widely used gas turbine for air transport aircraft.
notes.evidence: Turbofans are the most widely used gas turbine engine for air transport aircraft. The turbofan is a compromise between the good operating efficiency and high thrust capability of a turboprop and the high speed, high altitude capability of a turbojet.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbofan Engines”, p. 1-56

notes.front: A turbofan's fan moves 240 lb/sec around the core while 40 lb/sec passes through the core. What is its bypass ratio?
notes.explanation: Bypass ratio is fan bypass flow divided by core flow: 240 ÷ 40 = 6.
notes.choicesExplained: B divides total flow (280) by the core flow. C is the handbook's own worked example (100 ÷ 20), not these flows. D inverts the ratio.
notes.evidence: The amount of air flow in lb/sec from the fan bypass to the core flow of the engine is the bypass ratio.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: A turbofan moves 3 lb of fan air round its core for every pound through it. How is it classed?
notes.back: C: Medium-bypass
notes.explanation: A 3:1 bypass ratio lies between 2:1 and 4:1, the medium-bypass range.
notes.choices:
A) High-bypass
B) Low-bypass
C) Medium-bypass
D) Not a turbofan
notes.choicesExplained: A needs 4:1 or greater. B: 3:1 lies inside the 2:1 to 4:1 medium-bypass range, so it is not low-bypass. D: any engine with a fan bypass flow is a turbofan.
notes.evidence: Medium-bypass ratio engine. A turbofan engine whose bypass ratio is between 2:1 and 4:1.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Medium-bypass ratio engine”, p. G-18

notes.front: What share of a turboprop gas turbine's energy drives the propeller?
notes.back: Approximately 80 to 85 percent; the rest leaves the exhaust as thrust.
notes.explanation: Adding shaft horsepower to the horsepower in the exhaust thrust gives equivalent shaft horsepower.
notes.evidence: Approximately 80 to 85 percent of the energy developed by the gas turbine engine is used to drive the propeller. The rest of the available energy exits the exhaust as thrust. By adding the horsepower developed by the engine shaft and the horsepower in the exiting thrust, the answer is equivalent shaft horsepower.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-37

notes.front: Why is a turboshaft engine's output measured in horsepower rather than thrust?
notes.back: Because its power output is a turning shaft.
notes.explanation: It drives something other than a propeller through that shaft, so no jet thrust figure applies.
notes.evidence: The turboshaft engine's output is measured in horsepower instead of thrust because the power output is a turning shaft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboshaft Engines”, p. 1-55

notes.front: Which engine type is described: a gas turbine delivering power through a shaft to a helicopter's main rotor gearbox?
notes.back: C: Turboshaft
notes.explanation: A shaft driving something other than a propeller defines a turboshaft.
notes.choices:
A) Turbojet
B) Turbofan
C) Turboshaft
D) Turboprop
notes.choicesExplained: A makes thrust from exhaust velocity. B drives a ducted fan. D drives a propeller, which a helicopter rotor transmission is not.
notes.evidence: A gas-turbine engine that delivers power through a shaft to operate something other than a propeller is referred to as a turboshaft engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboshaft Engines”, p. 1-55

notes.front: How does a fixed-turbine turboprop differ from a free-turbine turboprop?
notes.back: Fixed: a mechanical connection from gas generator to reduction gearbox and propeller. Free: only an air link to the power turbines.
notes.explanation: In the free-turbine type there is no mechanical link from the propeller to the gas generator.
notes.evidence: The fixed turbine has a mechanical connection from the gas generator (gas-turbine engine) to the reduction gear box and propeller. The free turbine has only an air link from gas generator to the power turbines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboprop Engines”, p. 1-54

notes.front: On a turboprop, the propeller can be held still while the gas generator turns, since no shaft joins them. Which type is it?
notes.back: D: Free-turbine turboprop
notes.explanation: The free turbine has only an air link from the gas generator, with no mechanical link to the propeller.
notes.choices:
A) Geared turbofan
B) Fixed-turbine turboprop
C) Single-spool turbojet
D) Free-turbine turboprop
notes.choicesExplained: B has a mechanical connection from gas generator to propeller. C has no propeller. A is a turbofan, which drives a ducted fan, not a propeller.
notes.evidence: The free turbine has only an air link from gas generator to the power turbines. There is no mechanical link from the propeller to the gas turbine engine (gas generator).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turboprop Engines”, p. 1-54

notes.front: Why must a turbofan inlet have icing protection, and how is it provided?
notes.back: Ice on the inlet lip could break loose and damage the fan; warm compressor air is ducted through the inlet.
notes.explanation: On most modern turbofans the fan is the first part of the aircraft the incoming air meets.
notes.evidence: This prevents chunks of ice from forming on the leading edge of the inlet, breaking loose, and damaging the fan. Warm air is bled from the engine's compressor and is ducted through the inlet to prevent ice from forming.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Air Entrance”, p. 1-37

notes.front: What drives the gear train in a gas turbine accessory case?
notes.back: The engine high-pressure compressor, through an accessory drive shaft (tower shaft) gear coupling.
notes.explanation: The accessory reduction gear ratios are relatively high because the rotor operating rpm is so high.
notes.evidence: The gear train is driven by the engine high-pressure compressor through an accessory drive shaft (tower shaft) gear coupling, which splines with a gear box gear and the high-pressure compressor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Accessory Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: A trainee asks why accessory gear ratios on a gas turbine are so high compared with a piston engine. What is the answer?
notes.back: A: The rotor operating rpm is very high
notes.explanation: Reduction gearing brings the very high rotor speed down to suitable drive speeds for each accessory.
notes.choices:
A) The rotor operating rpm is very high
B) The accessories need more torque than the engine makes
C) The gearbox also acts as an oil reservoir
D) The tower shaft turns backwards
notes.choicesExplained: B is not the reason given. C is a secondary function of the case, not a gearing reason. D is invented.
notes.evidence: The reduction gearing within the case provides suitable drive speeds for each engine accessory or component. Because the rotor operating rpm is so high, the accessory reduction gear ratios are relatively high.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Accessory Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: What is the primary function of the compressor section?
notes.back: To supply air in sufficient quantity for the combustion burners, raising its pressure and delivering it at the quantity and pressures required.
notes.explanation: A secondary function is supplying bleed air for the engine and aircraft.
notes.evidence: Its primary function is to supply air in sufficient quantity to satisfy the requirements of the combustion burners. Specifically, to fulfill its purpose, the compressor must increase the pressure of the mass of air received from the air inlet duct
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: Which of these is a secondary function of the compressor section, not its primary one?
notes.back: B: Supplying bleed air for the engine and aircraft
notes.explanation: The handbook names bleed air as the compressor's secondary function.
notes.choices:
A) Raising the pressure of the air from the inlet duct
B) Supplying bleed air for the engine and aircraft
C) Discharging air to the burners at the pressure needed
D) Supplying enough air for the burners
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C all describe the primary function of feeding the burners.
notes.evidence: A secondary function of the compressor is to supply bleedair for various purposes in the engine and aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: What are the three components of a centrifugal-flow compressor?
notes.back: An impeller (rotor), a diffuser (stator) and a compressor manifold.
notes.explanation: The impeller and diffuser are the two main functional elements.
notes.evidence: The centrifugal-flow compressor consists of an impeller (rotor), a diffuser (stator), and a compressor manifold. [Figure 1-46] Centrifugal compressors have a high pressure rise per stage that can be around 8:1.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Centrifugal-Flow Compressors”, p. 1-38

notes.front: From inlet to exit of an axial-flow compressor, air is compressed at a ratio of approximately {{c1::1.25:1}} per stage.
notes.explanation: The small rise per stage is why axial compressors need many stages.
notes.evidence: From inlet to exit, the air flows along an axial path and is compressed at a ratio of approximately 1.25:1 per stage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-40

notes.front: What do the stator vanes of an axial-flow compressor do?
notes.back: Receive air from the inlet or preceding stage, raise its pressure, and deliver it to the next stage at the correct velocity and pressure.
notes.explanation: They also control the direction of air to each rotor stage for the best possible blade efficiency.
notes.evidence: The function of the stator vanes is to receive air from the air inlet duct or from each preceding stage and increase the pressure of the air and deliver it to the next stage at the correct velocity and pressure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-40

notes.front: What are two advantages of a centrifugal-flow compressor?
notes.back: Any two, among others: high pressure rise per stage; efficiency over a wide speed range; simple, low-cost manufacture.
notes.explanation: Low weight and low starting power are further advantages in the handbook's list.
notes.evidence: High pressure rise per stage, • Efficiency over wide rotational speed range, • Simplicity of manufacture and low cost,
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-42

notes.front: What are the two disadvantages of a centrifugal-flow compressor?
notes.back: A large frontal area for a given airflow, and losses in turns between stages.
notes.explanation: The axial compressor avoids turning losses by keeping air in its original direction.
notes.evidence: Its large frontal area for a given airflow and • Losses in turns between stages.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-43

notes.front: An engine designer needs the smallest possible frontal area for a large airflow on a fast jet. Which compressor type suits this best?
notes.back: B: Axial-flow
notes.explanation: Small frontal area for a given airflow is an axial-flow advantage.
notes.choices:
A) Single-stage centrifugal
B) Axial-flow
C) Double-entry centrifugal
D) Two-stage centrifugal
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are centrifugal, whose disadvantage is a large frontal area for a given airflow.
notes.evidence: Small frontal area for given airflow; • Straight-through flow, allowing high ram efficiency;
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-43

notes.front: Air enters a compressor at 14.7 psi and leaves at 220.5 psi. What is the compressor pressure ratio?
notes.explanation: Outlet pressure divided by inlet pressure: 220.5 ÷ 14.7 = 15.
notes.choicesExplained: A subtracts instead of dividing. B and D invert the ratio.
notes.evidence: This ratio is the outlet pressure divided by the inlet pressure.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Air Entrance”, p. 1-37

notes.front: How does a dual-spool engine differ from a single-spool engine?
notes.back: Single: the high-pressure turbine drives the whole compressor. Dual: compressor and turbine split in two, on two shafts, one inside the other.
notes.explanation: Each compressor segment is driven by its own turbine.
notes.evidence: In a single-spool engine, the highpressure turbine drives the entire compressor. In a dual-spool engine, the compressor and high-pressure turbine are both split into two segments. Each compressor segment is driven by its corresponding turbine using two separate drive shafts, with one inside the other.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-40

notes.front: In a two-spool turbofan, what does each spool contain?
notes.back: Low-pressure spool: the fan(s) and the turbine stages driving them. High-pressure spool: the high-pressure compressor, shaft and turbines.
notes.explanation: The high-pressure spool is the core of the engine, where the combustion section sits.
notes.evidence: The low-pressure spool generally contains the fan(s) and the turbine stages it takes to drive them. The high-pressure spool is the high-pressure compressor, shaft, and turbines. This spool makes up the core of the engine, and this is where the combustion section is located.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: On a two-spool turbofan, a mechanic traces which turbine drives the fan. Which spool is it on?
notes.back: B: The low-pressure spool
notes.explanation: The low-pressure spool generally holds the fan and the turbine stages that drive it.
notes.choices:
A) The high-pressure spool
B) The low-pressure spool
C) A free turbine on the high-pressure shaft
D) The accessory gearbox
notes.choicesExplained: A is the core spool with the high-pressure compressor. D is driven by the engine, it drives no fan. C is not how the handbook describes a two-spool turbofan.
notes.evidence: In a two-spool engine, there is a high-pressure spool and a lowpressure spool. The low-pressure spool generally contains the fan(s) and the turbine stages it takes to drive them.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-36

notes.front: Why do inlet guide vanes give entering air a preswirl in the direction of engine rotation?
notes.back: It improves the compressor's aerodynamic characteristics by reducing drag on the first-stage rotor blades.
notes.explanation: The vanes also direct the air into the first-stage rotor blades at the proper angle.
notes.evidence: The guide vanes direct the airflow into the first stage rotor blades at the proper angle and impart a swirling motion to the air entering the compressor. This preswirl, in the direction of engine rotation, improves the aerodynamic characteristics of the compressor by reducing drag on the first stage rotor blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-40

notes.front: What is the main difference between variable inlet guide vanes and variable stator vanes?
notes.back: Their position: variable inlet guide vanes sit in front of the rotor blades; variable stator vanes sit behind them.
notes.explanation: One version of the single-spool compressor uses both, with the first few rows of stator vanes variable.
notes.evidence: The main difference between variable inlet guide vane (VIGV) and a variable stator vane (VSV) is their position with regard to the rotor blades. VIGV are in front of the rotor blades, and VSV are behind the rotor blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-41

notes.front: On an engine with variable inlet guide vanes and variable stator vanes, what sets their angles in operation?
notes.back: D: The power lever position, in relation to the power required
notes.explanation: The vane angles are variables controlled in direct relation to the power the engine must produce.
notes.choices:
A) Fixed by the manufacturer and never changed
B) Only the ambient temperature
C) The mechanic, at each inspection
D) The power lever position, in relation to the power required
notes.choicesExplained: B names one input only. C: they vary during operation, not at inspection. A describes fixed vanes.
notes.evidence: These variables are controlled in direct relation to the amount of power the engine is required to produce by the power lever position.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Axial-Flow Compressor”, p. 1-42

notes.front: If compressor discharge air reached the flame area without being slowed, what could happen?
notes.back: D: The flame could be extinguished
notes.explanation: The diffuser slows the air so the flame can burn continuously.
notes.choices:
A) The compressor would stall at once
B) The fuel would fail to atomise
C) The turbine would overspeed
D) The flame could be extinguished
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are not what the handbook links to fast air in the flame area.
notes.evidence: If the air passed through the flame area at a high velocity, it could extinguish the flame.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Diffuser”, p. 1-43

notes.front: What does secondary (cooling) air do in a combustion chamber, and by how much?
notes.back: It passes between casing and liner and joins the gases through rear holes, cooling them from about 3,500 °F to near 1,500 °F.
notes.explanation: The larger holes toward the rear of the liner admit it after combustion.
notes.evidence: Secondary or cooling air passes between the outer casing and the liner and joins the combustion gases through larger holes toward the rear of the liner, cooling the combustion gases from about 3,500 °F to near 1,500 °F.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-44

notes.front: Why must a combustion chamber drain unburned fuel after shutdown?
notes.back: To prevent gum deposits in the manifold, nozzles and chambers, and above all the danger of afterfire at the next start.
notes.explanation: Fuel left in the chamber can ignite at the next start and exceed safe exhaust gas temperature limits.
notes.evidence: Probably most important is the danger of afterfire if the fuel is allowed to accumulate after shutdown. If the fuel is not drained, a great possibility exists that, at the next starting attempt, the excess fuel in the combustion chamber will ignite
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-44

notes.front: A combustion drain is found blocked after a series of shutdowns. What is the most important risk at the next start?
notes.back: B: Accumulated fuel igniting and exceeding safe exhaust temperature limits
notes.explanation: The handbook calls afterfire from accumulated fuel probably the most important reason for draining.
notes.choices:
A) Lean flameout at idle
B) Accumulated fuel igniting and exceeding safe exhaust temperature limits
C) Compressor inducer damage
D) Loss of bleed air pressure
notes.choicesExplained: A is caused by too little fuel, not stored fuel. C comes from foreign objects. D is unrelated to fuel drainage.
notes.evidence: the excess fuel in the combustion chamber will ignite and exhaust gas temperature will exceed safe operating limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-44

notes.front: Which type of combustion chamber do modern turbine engines usually have?
notes.back: The annular combustion chamber.
notes.explanation: It uses louvres and holes to keep the flame off the sides of the chamber.
notes.evidence: Modern turbine engines usually have an annular combustion chamber.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: Which combustor type reverses the airflow twice, and where is it used?
notes.back: The reverse-flow combustor; it is used where engine length is critical.
notes.explanation: Air enters the outer case, reverses into the inner liner, then reverses again before the turbine.
notes.evidence: A reverse-flow combustor is a type of combustor in which the air from the compressor enters the combustor outer case and reverses its direction as it flows into the inner liner. It again reverses its direction before it flows through the turbine. Reverse-flow combustors are used where engine length is critical.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: A small turboshaft has separate burners, each a perforated stainless liner inside its own removable outer case. Which combustor type is it?
notes.back: A: Can-type
notes.explanation: Separate chambers each with an outer case and perforated liner, typical of turboshafts, are can-type.
notes.choices:
A) Can-type
B) Annular
C) Reverse-flow
D) Can-annular
notes.choicesExplained: B has one undivided circular liner. C is defined by air reversing direction. D mounts its cans on a shared annular duct.
notes.evidence: Each of the can-type combustion chambers consists of an outer case or housing, within which there is a perforated stainless steel (highly heat resistant) combustion chamber liner or inner liner.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-43

notes.front: A modern turbofan has one undivided liner encircling the turbine shaft housing, coated with ceramic thermal barrier. Which combustor type is it?
notes.back: B: Annular
notes.explanation: An undivided circular shroud round the turbine shaft housing is the annular chamber's liner.
notes.choices:
A) Can-annular
B) Annular
C) Can-type
D) Reverse-flow
notes.choicesExplained: A and C use separate cans. D is identified by its double reversal of airflow, not by an undivided liner.
notes.evidence: The chamber is constructed of heat-resistant materials, which are sometimes coated with thermal barrier materials, such as ceramic materials. The annular combustion chamber is illustrated in Figure 1-58. Modern turbine engines usually have an annular combustion chamber.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Combustion Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: Why must turbine inlet temperature be controlled?
notes.back: The turbine inlet nozzle vanes meet the highest temperature that contacts metal in the engine, and they will be damaged otherwise.
notes.explanation: The vanes sit directly aft of the combustion chambers, just ahead of the turbine wheel.
notes.evidence: This is the highest or hottest temperature that comes in contact with metal components in the engine. The turbine inlet temperature must be controlled, or damage will occur to the turbine inlet vanes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-46

notes.front: What are the two purposes of the turbine inlet nozzle?
notes.back: To convert heat and pressure energy to velocity energy, and to deflect the gases toward the direction of turbine rotation.
notes.explanation: The gas must enter the blade passages while they are still rotating, so it is aimed that way.
notes.evidence: The second purpose of the turbine inlet nozzle is to deflect the gases to a specific angle in the direction of turbine wheel rotation. Since the gas flow from the nozzle must enter the turbine blade passageway while it is still rotating, it is essential to aim the gas in the general direction of turbine rotation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: On a nozzle assembly with welded vanes, a mechanic sees the outer shroud ring cut into segments by saw cuts. What are the cuts for?
notes.back: B: Allowing thermal expansion without stress and warping of the vanes
notes.explanation: Welded vanes cannot move in their shrouds, so one ring is segmented to allow expansion.
notes.choices:
A) Balancing the assembly
B) Allowing thermal expansion without stress and warping of the vanes
C) Draining unburned fuel
D) Letting cooling air into the vanes
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are not what the handbook gives as the purpose of the segmenting cuts.
notes.evidence: The saw cuts separating the segments allow sufficient expansion to prevent stress and warping of the vanes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: Why must engine speed and temperature be controlled to keep the turbine within safe limits?
notes.back: High speed imposes severe centrifugal loads on the wheel while high temperature lowers the strength of its material.
notes.explanation: The two effects act at the same time on the turbine wheel.
notes.evidence: The high rotational speed imposes severe centrifugal loads on the turbine wheel, and at the same time the elevated temperatures result in a lowering of the strength of the material. Consequently, the engine speed and temperature must be controlled to keep turbine operation within safe limits.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: What makes up a turbine stage, and why are several stages sometimes needed?
notes.back: A row of stationary vanes (nozzles) followed by a row of rotating blades; one wheel often cannot absorb enough power.
notes.explanation: Regardless of the number of wheels, a turbine nozzle always precedes each wheel.
notes.evidence: A single turbine wheel often cannot absorb enough power from the exhaust gases to drive the components dependent on the turbine for rotative power; thus, it is necessary to add additional turbine stages. A turbine stage consists of a row of stationary vanes or nozzles, followed by a row of rotating blades.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-50

notes.front: With the engine cold, a mechanic finds the turbine blades move slightly in their disc slots. What should be concluded?
notes.back: A: Normal: disc expansion in operation makes the roots fit tightly
notes.explanation: Clearance at the blade root is deliberate so the disc can expand; it closes when hot.
notes.choices:
A) This is normal: disc expansion in operation makes the roots fit tightly
B) The disc has stretched from overspeed
C) The blades were installed in the wrong slots
D) The blade retention has failed and the wheel must be rejected
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C read a designed-in cold clearance as a defect.
notes.evidence: Sufficient clearance exists between the blade root and the notch to permit movement of the turbine blade when the disc is cold. During engine operation, expansion of the disc decreases the clearance. This causes the blade root to fit tightly in the disc rim.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-49

notes.front: Which type of turbine blade is also called a bucket?
notes.back: The impulse turbine blade.
notes.explanation: The gas strikes the centre of the blade and changes direction, which turns the disc.
notes.evidence: The impulse turbine blade is also referred to as a bucket. This is because as the stream of air strikes the center of the blade it changes the direction of the energy as it causes the blades to rotate the disc and rotor shaft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: Which type of turbine blade turns the disc by the aerodynamic action of gas flowing past it at a set angle?
notes.back: The reaction turbine blade.
notes.explanation: The angle is chosen to develop the most efficient power from the engine.
notes.evidence: Reaction turbine blades cause the disc to rotate by the aerodynamic action of the airstream directed to flow past the blade at a particular angle in order to develop the most efficient power from the turbine engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: What shape is a reaction-impulse turbine blade?
notes.back: Bucket-shaped like an impulse blade at the root, and aerofoil-shaped like a reaction blade toward the tip.
notes.explanation: It combines the actions of both designs along its length.
notes.evidence: The blade has more of the bucket shape of the impulse blade at the blade root and it also has more of an airfoil shape of the reaction blade on the second half of the blade toward the outer end of the blade.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: A turbine blade is cupped at its root but twisted into an aerofoil toward its tip. Which blade type is it?
notes.back: B: Reaction-impulse
notes.explanation: A bucket root with an aerofoil outer half combines both designs.
notes.choices:
A) Impulse
B) Reaction-impulse
C) Reaction
D) Shrouded
notes.choicesExplained: A is bucket-shaped throughout. C is an aerofoil throughout. D describes tip bands, not the blade's working action.
notes.evidence: The reaction-impulse turbine blade combines the action of both the impulse and reaction blades designs.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-47

notes.front: A designer wants the highest possible turbine speed with the fewest blades. Which blade tip design suits this?
notes.back: B: Open (unshrouded) blades
notes.explanation: Most turbines are open at the tips; shrouding trades speed and blade count for efficiency and vibration benefits.
notes.choices:
A) Shrouded blades
B) Open (unshrouded) blades
C) Shrouded blades with more stages
D) Either; tip design does not affect speed
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: shrouds limit turbine speed and require more blades. D ignores that limit.
notes.evidence: Most turbines are open at the outer perimeter of the blades; however, a second type called the shrouded turbine is sometimes used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Turbine Section”, p. 1-50

notes.front: What are the components of a gas turbine exhaust section?
notes.back: The exhaust cone, the tailpipe (if required) and the exhaust nozzle.
notes.explanation: The exhaust cone assembly ends the basic engine; the nozzle is usually an airframe component.
notes.evidence: The components of the exhaust section include the exhaust cone, tailpipe (if required), and the exhaust nozzle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Exhaust Section”, p. 1-51

notes.front: What two functions do the radial struts in the exhaust cone assembly have?
notes.back: They support the inner cone and straighten the swirling exhaust gases, which would otherwise leave the turbine at about 45°.
notes.explanation: Some assemblies use the hollow struts as the sole support for the inner cone.
notes.evidence: exhaust duct, but they also perform the important function of straightening the swirling exhaust gases that would otherwise leave the turbine at an angle of approximately 45°.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Exhaust Section”, p. 1-51

notes.front: A fixed-area exhaust nozzle of the wrong, too-small size is fitted. What could result?
notes.back: D: The engine could choke or stall
notes.explanation: A fixed nozzle's outlet area is very critical to engine performance.
notes.choices:
A) Wasted thrust only
B) Nothing, as area is not critical
C) Lower exhaust gas velocity and no other effect
D) The engine could choke or stall
notes.choicesExplained: A is the effect of a nozzle that is too large. C does not follow from the source. B contradicts it: outlet area is very critical.
notes.evidence: The outlet area of the fixed exhaust nozzle is very critical to engine performance. If the nozzle area is too large, thrust is wasted; if the area is too small, the engine could choke or stall.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Exhaust Section”, p. 1-52

notes.front: What is the minimum bearing arrangement needed to support one gas turbine shaft?
notes.back: One deep groove ball bearing (thrust and radial loads) and one straight roller bearing (radial load only).
notes.explanation: More roller bearings may be needed if the shaft vibrates or is very long.
notes.evidence: The minimum number of bearings required to support one shaft is one deep groove ball bearing (thrust and radial loads) and one straight roller bearing (radial load only).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Bearings & Seals”, p. 1-52

notes.front: What are the main disadvantages of the antifriction (ball and roller) bearings used on gas turbine rotors?
notes.back: Vulnerability to foreign matter, and a tendency to fail without appreciable warning.
notes.explanation: They are otherwise preferred for low resistance, easy replacement and tolerance of overloads and heat.
notes.evidence: The main disadvantages are their vulnerability to foreign matter and tendency to fail without appreciable warning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Bearings & Seals”, p. 1-53

notes.front: Which main bearing on a gas turbine shaft is positioned to absorb the axial (thrust) loads?
notes.back: C: The ball bearing
notes.explanation: Ball bearings are placed so they can absorb axial or radial loads.
notes.choices:
A) The roller bearing
B) The carbon seal
C) The ball bearing
D) The labyrinth seal
notes.choicesExplained: A: roller bearings are better at radial than thrust loads and are used mainly for those. B and D are oil seals, not bearings.
notes.evidence: Usually the ball bearings are positioned on the compressor or turbine shaft so that they can absorb any axial (thrust) loads or radial loads. Because the roller bearings present a larger working surface, they are better equipped to support radial loads than thrust loads.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Bearings & Seals”, p. 1-53

notes.front: How does a labyrinth oil seal differ from a helical (thread) seal?
notes.back: The labyrinth seal is usually pressurised; the helical seal relies solely on reverse threading to stop oil leakage.
notes.explanation: Otherwise they are very similar, differing only in thread size and pressurisation.
notes.evidence: The labyrinth seal is usually pressurized, but the helical seal depends solely on reverse threading to stop oil leakage. These two types of seals are very similar, differing only in thread size and the fact that the labyrinth seal is pressurized.
