notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Gas Turbine Engine Bearings & Seals”, p. 1-53

notes.front: Which part belongs to the cold section of a gas turbine engine?
notes.back: D: Diffuser
notes.explanation: The cold section is everything ahead of the combustion section: inlet, compressor and diffuser.
notes.choices:
A) Turbine nozzle
B) Exhaust cone
C) Combustion liner
D) Diffuser
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are in the turbine, exhaust and combustion sections, which make up the hot section.
notes.evidence: Cold section. The portion of a gas turbine engine ahead of the combustion section. The cold section includes the inlet, compressor, and diffuser.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Cold section”, p. G-7

notes.front: How does dirt build-up on compressor blades affect a turbine engine?
notes.back: It reduces the blades' aerodynamic efficiency, like icing on a wing, deteriorating performance; slow acceleration and high exhaust temperature can follow.
notes.explanation: Centrifugal force throws dirt outward to coat the casing, vanes and blades.
notes.evidence: Accumulation of dirt on the compressor blades reduces the aerodynamic efficiency of the blades with resultant deterioration in engine performance. The efficiency of the blades is impaired by dirt deposits in a manner similar to that of an aircraft wing under icing conditions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-45

notes.front: What compressor blade edge damage is usually acceptable without rework?
notes.back: Well-rounded leading or trailing edge damage in the outer half only, within the manufacturer's indentation limits.
notes.explanation: Damage in the inner half must be treated with extreme caution.
notes.evidence: Well-rounded damage to leading and trailing edges that is evident on the opposite side of the blade is usually acceptable without re-work, provided the damage is in the outer half of the blade only, and the indentation does not exceed values specified in the engine manufacturer's service and overhaul instruction manuals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Inspection & Cleaning”, p. 10-45

notes.front: How are repaired compressor blades inspected, and what cracking is allowed?
notes.back: By magnetic particle or fluorescent penetrant inspection; no cracks of any extent are tolerated anywhere.
notes.explanation: The inspection confirms every trace of the damage has been removed.
notes.evidence: Repaired compressor blades are inspected by either magnetic particle or fluorescent penetrant inspection methods to ensure that all traces of the damage have been removed. All repairs must be well blended so that surfaces are smooth. [Figure 10-58] No cracks of any extent are tolerated in any area.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Inspection & Cleaning”, p. 10-45

notes.front: A mechanic plans to buff the whole surface of a nicked compressor blade with a power tool. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: C: Rework by hand; never power-buff the whole blade
notes.explanation: Rework is done by hand, locally, and parallel to the blade length where possible.
notes.choices:
A) Acceptable if the finish matches a new blade
B) Acceptable on the inner half only
C) Rework by hand with stones, files or emery cloth; never power-buff the whole blade
D) Use a power tool, then straighten the blade
notes.choicesExplained: A and B ignore the ban on power-buffing the whole area. D adds straightening, which is not a permitted repair.
notes.evidence: Whenever possible, stoning and local re-work of the blade should be performed parallel to the length of the blade. Rework must be accomplished by hand, using stones, files, or emery cloth. Do not use a power tool to buff the entire area of the blade.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Inspection & Cleaning”, p. 10-45

notes.front: What personal precaution does the handbook give for working around operating turbine engines?
notes.back: Do not carry any objects in your pockets.
notes.explanation: Items such as pencils, tools and flashlights are often drawn into the engine and damage the fan blades.
notes.evidence: Foreign object damage (FOD), such as pencils, tools, and flashlights, are often drawn into the engine and can cause damage to the fan blades. [Figure 10-59] Do not carry any objects in pockets when working around operational turbine engines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Causes of Blade Damage”, p. 10-45

notes.front: What simple measure guards against tools left in an air intake?
notes.back: Checking the tools against a tool checklist.
notes.explanation: Tools left in the intake are drawn in on later starts and can damage the compressor rotor beyond repair.
notes.evidence: A compressor rotor can be damaged beyond repair by tools that are left in the air intake, where they are drawn into the engine on subsequent starts. A simple solution to the problem is to check the tools against a tool checklist.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Causes of Blade Damage”, p. 10-45

notes.front: After an intake repair, the tool board shows one screwdriver missing. The run-up is due now. What should happen first?
notes.back: B: Find the tool, checking the inlet duct, before any start
notes.explanation: Checking tools against a checklist and inspecting the inlet before starting prevent this damage.
notes.choices:
A) Start the engine at idle; small items pass through
B) Find the tool, checking the inlet duct, before any start
C) Run at high power to clear the intake
D) Log the missing tool and run the engine
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C risk the tool being drawn in, which can damage the compressor rotor beyond repair.
notes.evidence: A compressor rotor can be damaged beyond repair by tools that are left in the air intake, where they are drawn into the engine on subsequent starts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Causes of Blade Damage”, p. 10-45

notes.front: Which repair methods must never be used on a compressor vane?
notes.back: Straightening, brazing, welding or soldering.
notes.explanation: Damage is blended out instead with crocus cloth, fine files and stones.
notes.evidence: Do not attempt to repair any vane by straightening, brazing, welding, or soldering. Crocus cloth, fine files, and stones are used to blend out damage by removing a minimum of material and leaving a surface finish comparable to that of a new part.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Causes of Blade Damage”, p. 10-45

notes.front: What is the purpose of blending out blade damage?
notes.back: To minimise the stresses that concentrate at dents, scratches or cracks.
notes.explanation: Removing a minimum of material with a new-part finish leaves no sharp stress raiser.
notes.evidence: The purpose of this blending is to minimize stresses that concentrate at dents, scratches, or cracks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Causes of Blade Damage”, p. 10-45

notes.front: A guide vane shows a crack that forks so a piece of metal could break free into the compressor. What is the action?
notes.back: C: Reject the vane
notes.explanation: Forked or branched cracks that could release metal into the compressor mean rejection.
notes.choices:
A) Braze the crack
B) Blend it out and return to service
C) Reject the vane
D) Accept it if the crack is on the leading edge
notes.choicesExplained: B and A repair a crack the source treats as rejectable, and brazing vanes is not allowed. D has no basis in the source.
notes.evidence: Cracks that branch or fork out so that a piece of metal could break free and fall into the compressor are cause for vane rejection.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Blending & Replacement”, p. 10-47

notes.front: In blade maintenance terms, what is a burr and its usual cause?
notes.back: A ragged or turned-out edge, usually from a grinding or cutting operation.
notes.explanation: The handbook table pairs each damage term with its appearance and usual causes.
notes.evidence: Burr • A ragged or turned out edge. • Grinding or cutting operation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

image.alt: Table of blade damage terms. Burr: ragged or turned-out edge, from grinding or cutting. Corrosion (pits): pitted surface, from corrosive agents such as moisture. Crack: partial fracture, from excessive stress, overloading, faulty processing, defective materials or overheating. Dent: small smoothly rounded hollow, from striking with a dull object. Gall: metal transferred between surfaces, from severe rubbing. Gouging: material displaced with a cutting or tearing effect, from a large foreign body between moving parts. Growth: blade elongation, from continued or excessive heat and centrifugal force. Score: deep scratches, from chips between surfaces. Scratch: narrow shallow marks, from sand or fine particles or careless handling. Burning: discoloured surface, from excessive heat.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), Figure 10-61

notes.front: In blade maintenance terms, what is a dent and its usual cause?
notes.back: A small, smoothly rounded hollow, from a part being struck by a dull object.
notes.explanation: A dent displaces metal without removing it, unlike a gouge.
notes.evidence: Striking of a part with a dull object. • Dent • Small, smoothly rounded hollow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

notes.front: In blade maintenance terms, what is galling and its usual cause?
notes.back: A transfer of metal from one surface to another, from severe rubbing.
notes.explanation: Galling appears where two surfaces rub hard enough to move metal between them.
notes.evidence: Gall • A transfer of metal from one surface to another. • Severe rubbing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

notes.front: In blade maintenance terms, what is scoring and its usual cause?
notes.back: Deep scratches, from chips present between surfaces.
notes.explanation: Scoring is deeper than a scratch.
notes.evidence: Score • Deep scratches. • Presence of chips between surfaces.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

notes.front: A blade is found slightly longer than its neighbours after long running at high temperature. Which damage term fits?
notes.back: C: Growth
notes.explanation: Growth is elongation of the blade, from continued or excessive heat and centrifugal force.
notes.choices:
A) Gouging
B) Burr
C) Growth
D) Bow
notes.choicesExplained: A is material torn away by a large foreign body. B is a ragged edge from grinding or cutting. D is a bent blade.
notes.evidence: Growth • Elongation of blade. • Presence of a comparatively large foreign body between moving parts. • Continued and/or excessive heat and centrifugal force.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

notes.front: A fan blade shows material torn out of its surface after a bolt lodged between moving parts. Which damage term fits?
notes.back: A: Gouging
notes.explanation: Gouging is displacement of material with a cutting or tearing effect.
notes.choices:
A) Gouging
B) Scratch
C) Dent
D) Gall
notes.choicesExplained: B is narrow shallow marks. C is a smooth hollow with no material removed. D is metal transferred by rubbing.
notes.evidence: Gouging • Displacement of material from a surface; a cutting or tearing effect.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Compressor Section”, p. 10-48

notes.front: What does the handbook call one of the controlling factors in a turbine engine's service life?
notes.back: The inspection and cleaning of the hot section.
notes.explanation: This is why careful inspection and repair of the hot section is emphasised.
notes.evidence: One of the controlling factors in the service life of the turbine engine is the inspection and cleaning of the hot section. Emphasis must be placed on the importance of careful inspection and repair of this section.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Combustion Section Inspection”, p. 10-47

notes.front: What is checked on the external combustion case before it is opened?
notes.back: Evidence of hot spots, exhaust leaks and distortions.
notes.explanation: Once opened, the chambers are checked for localised overheating, cracks or excessive wear.
notes.evidence: The entire external combustion case should be inspected for evidence of hot spots, exhaust leaks, and distortions before the case is opened.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Combustion Section Inspection”, p. 10-47

notes.front: A turboprop operates daily from a coastal strip exposed to salt spray. What hot section cleaning does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: B: A turbine rinse
notes.explanation: Hot section cleaning is not usually needed in the field, except in areas of high salt water or other chemicals.
notes.choices:
A) None; hot sections are never cleaned in the field
B) A turbine rinse
C) Strip and degrease the hot section weekly
D) Blend all turbine blades
notes.choicesExplained: A overstates the rule: cleaning is not usually necessary, but salt areas are the exception. C and D are not what the source prescribes.
notes.evidence: Cleaning the hot section is not usually necessary for a repair in the field, but in areas of high salt water or other chemicals a turbine rinse should be accomplished.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Combustion Section Inspection”, p. 10-47

notes.front: Where may a wax marking pencil be used on a turbine engine?
notes.back: Only on parts not directly exposed to the gas path; never on a liner surface or turbine rotor.
notes.explanation: Gas path parts are marked with layout dye, felt tip marker or chalk instead.
notes.evidence: A wax marking pencil may be used for parts that are not directly exposed to the gas path. Do not use a wax marking pencil on a liner surface or a turbine rotor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Marking Materials for Combustion Section Parts”, p. 10-49

notes.front: Why are carbon alloy or metallic pencils not recommended for marking hot section parts?
notes.back: They could cause intergranular corrosion attack, reducing material strength and causing cracking.
notes.explanation: The risk is to the metal itself, not just the visibility of the mark.
notes.evidence: The use of carbon alloy or metallic pencils is not recommended because of the possibility of causing intergranular corrosion attack, that could result in a reduction in material strength and cracking.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Marking Materials for Combustion Section Parts”, p. 10-49

notes.front: During a hot section inspection, a mechanic must mark positions on first-stage turbine blades. Which marker is acceptable?
notes.back: A: Chalk
notes.explanation: Chalk, a felt tip marker or light layout dye may mark gas path parts.
notes.choices:
A) Chalk
B) A wax marking pencil
C) A metallic scribe
D) A graphite (lead) pencil
notes.choicesExplained: D and C are carbon or metallic pencils that risk intergranular corrosion. B must not be used on a turbine rotor.
notes.evidence: directly exposed to the engine's gas path, such as turbine blades and discs, turbine vanes, and combustion chamber liners.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Marking Materials for Combustion Section Parts”, p. 10-49

notes.front: Two cracks run in from a free edge of a combustion chamber and are about to meet. What must be done?
notes.back: A: Repair or replace the chamber
notes.explanation: Meeting cracks could release a piece of metal that damages the turbine.
notes.choices:
A) Repair or replace the chamber
B) Stop-drill and return to service
C) Accept it; cracks at free edges are normal
D) Note it for the next overhaul
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D leave a piece of metal free to break loose and damage the turbine.
notes.evidence: Combustion chambers should be replaced or repaired if two cracks are progressing from a free edge so that their meeting is imminent and could allow a piece of metal that could cause turbine damage to break loose.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Inspection & Repair of Combustion Chambers”, p. 10-49

notes.front: What happens if a crack is found on a turbine disc?
notes.back: The disc is rejected and the turbine rotor replaced.
notes.explanation: Any disc crack means rejection; only slight pitting from foreign matter may be blended by stoning and polishing.
notes.evidence: Cracks on the disc necessitate the rejection of the disc and replacement of the turbine rotor. Slight pitting caused by the impingement of foreign matter may be blended by stoning and polishing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Disc Inspection”, p. 10-50

notes.front: What do stress rupture cracks on turbine blades usually look like?
notes.back: Minute hairline cracks on or across the leading or trailing edge, at a right angle to the edge length.
notes.explanation: Visible cracks may range from one-sixteenth inch upward, so a strong light and magnifier are used.
notes.evidence: Stress rupture cracks usually appear as minute hairline cracks on or across the leading or trailing edge at a right angle to the edge length. Visible cracks may range in length from one-sixteenth inch upward.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Blade Inspection”, p. 10-50

notes.front: Hairline cracks across the leading edges of several first-stage turbine blades are found. What must be suspected, and checked?
notes.back: C: Over-temperature; check blade stretch and disc hardness and stretch
notes.explanation: Stress rupture cracks or leading-edge deformation on first-stage blades point to over-temperature.
notes.choices:
A) Foreign object damage; blend the blades
B) Normal wear; no action
C) An over-temperature condition; check blades for stretch and the disc for hardness and stretch
D) A fuel nozzle leak; clean the nozzles
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses stress rupture cracks with impingement damage. B ignores the cracks. D addresses a different defect.
notes.evidence: When any stress rupture cracks or deformation of the leading edges of the first-stage turbine blades are found, an over-temperature condition must be suspected. Check the individual blades for stretch and the turbine disc for hardness and stretch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Blade Inspection”, p. 10-51

notes.front: When turbine blades are removed for detailed inspection, how must they be refitted?
notes.back: In the same slots from which they were removed, so they are numbered before removal.
notes.explanation: This also applies to blades removed to check turbine disc stretch.
notes.evidence: Blades removed for a detailed inspection or for a check of turbine disc stretch must be re-installed in the same slots from which they were removed. Number the blades prior to removal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Blade Inspection”, p. 10-51

notes.front: If a turbine blade's outer shroud shows air seal wear thinner than the specified limit, what is done?
notes.back: The stretched blade must be replaced.
notes.explanation: The worn shroud thickness is measured with a micrometer or similar at the bottom of the wear groove.
notes.evidence: If the remaining radial thickness of the shroud is less than that specified, the stretched blade must be replaced.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Blade Inspection”, p. 10-51

notes.front: One turbine blade must be replaced. What else must be replaced with it?
notes.back: A: The diametrically opposite blade
notes.explanation: Blades are installed by moment-weight in coded pairs, so they are replaced in pairs.
notes.choices:
A) The diametrically opposite blade
B) The two neighbouring blades
C) The whole turbine assembly
D) Nothing else
notes.choicesExplained: B is not the rule. C may be more economical only when several blades are damaged. D ignores the balance rule.
notes.evidence: If a blade requires replacement, the diametrically opposite blade must also be replaced.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Blade Replacement Procedure”, p. 10-52

notes.front: When are nicks in turbine nozzle vanes not cause for rejection?
notes.back: When they are small and blend out smoothly.
notes.explanation: If more vanes are damaged than the maximum replaceable, a new nozzle vane assembly is installed.
notes.evidence: Inspect the nozzle vanes for nicks or cracks. Small nicks are not cause for vane rejection, provided such nicks blend out smoothly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Nozzle Inlet Guide Vane Inspection”, p. 10-52

notes.front: Hot spots are found on an engine's tail cone during inspection. What do they indicate?
notes.back: D: A malfunctioning fuel nozzle or combustion chamber
notes.explanation: The exhaust section is inspected along with the combustion and turbine sections for this reason.
notes.choices:
A) An exhaust nozzle that is too large
B) Worn main bearings
C) A dirty compressor
D) A malfunctioning fuel nozzle or combustion chamber
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A are not linked to tail cone hot spots in the source.
notes.evidence: Inspect the exhaust cone and exhaust nozzle for cracks, warping, buckling, or hot spots. Hot spots on the tail cone are a good indication of a malfunctioning fuel nozzle or combustion chamber.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Exhaust Section”, p. 10-54

notes.front: What is the normal starting sequence for a turbine engine?
notes.back: Rotate the compressor with the starter; turn the ignition on; open the engine fuel valve.
notes.explanation: Following the prescribed procedure avoids a hot or hung start.
notes.evidence: Rotate the compressor with the starter; 2. Turn the ignition on; and 3. Open the engine fuel valve, either by moving the throttle to idle or by moving a fuel shutoff lever or turning a switch.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turbine Engine Operation”, p. 10-57

notes.front: During a turbine start, an engine fire occurs or the fire warning light comes on. What is the first action?
notes.back: Move the fuel shutoff lever to off, then keep cranking or motoring until the fire is expelled.
notes.explanation: Motoring the engine blows the fire out of it.
notes.evidence: Move the fuel shutoff lever to the off position if an engine fire occurs, or if the fire warning light is illuminated during the starting cycle. Continue cranking or motoring the engine until the fire has been expelled from the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Ground Operation Engine Fire”, p. 10-57

notes.front: If an engine fire persists while cranking, where should carbon dioxide be discharged?
notes.back: Into the inlet duct while the engine is cranked; never directly into the exhaust.
notes.explanation: Discharging it directly into the engine exhaust may damage the engine.
notes.evidence: If the fire persists, CO2 can be discharged into the inlet duct while it is being cranked. Do not discharge CO2 directly into the engine exhaust, because it may damage the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Ground Operation Engine Fire”, p. 10-57

notes.front: Burning fuel drips from the overboard drain onto the ground under a turbine engine. Where should the extinguishing agent go?
notes.back: B: On the ground, not on the engine
notes.explanation: The fire is on the ground, so that is where the agent goes.
notes.choices:
A) Into the engine exhaust
B) On the ground, not on the engine
C) Into the compressor bleed ports
D) Onto the engine cowling
notes.choicesExplained: A may damage the engine. C is not an extinguishing point. D targets the engine rather than the burning fuel.
notes.evidence: If the fire is on the ground under the engine overboard drain, discharge the CO2 on the ground rather than on the engine. This also is true if the fire is at the tailpipe and the fuel is dripping to the ground and burning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Ground Operation Engine Fire”, p. 10-57

notes.front: How is takeoff thrust checked on a turbofan?
notes.back: By adjusting the throttle to a single predicted engine pressure ratio reading, from a takeoff thrust setting curve or onboard computer.
notes.explanation: The value represents takeoff thrust for the prevailing ambient atmospheric conditions.
notes.evidence: Takeoff thrust is checked by adjusting the throttle to obtain a single, predicted reading on the engine pressure ratio indicator in the aircraft. The value for engine pressure ratio, which represents takeoff thrust for the prevailing ambient atmospheric conditions, is calculated from a takeoff thrust setting curve or, on newer aircraft, is a function of the onboard computer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Checking Takeoff Thrust”, p. 10-57

notes.front: A crew wants to check takeoff thrust while taxiing to save time. Why is that wrong for a precise check?
notes.back: B: The curve is computed for static conditions, so the aircraft must be stationary and stable
notes.explanation: Precise thrust checking needs the static conditions the curve assumes.
notes.choices:
A) Taxiing overheats the brakes
B) The thrust setting curve is computed for static conditions, so the aircraft should be stationary and stable
C) Thrust cannot be read while moving
D) Ram recovery is highest when stationary
notes.choicesExplained: A is not the reason given. C is untrue; the reading is shown at any time. D misstates ram recovery, which needs forward speed.
notes.evidence: This curve has been computed for static conditions. [Figure 10-74] Therefore, for all precise thrust checking, the aircraft should be stationary, and stable engine operation should be established.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Checking Takeoff Thrust”, p. 10-57

notes.front: When computing takeoff thrust for a stationary aircraft, which pressure must be used?
notes.back: The static field (true barometric) pressure, not the sea-level-corrected altimeter setting from the tower.
notes.explanation: The engine senses the actual pressure at its compressor inlet.
notes.evidence: When the aircraft is stationary, the pressure at the compressor inlet is the static field or true barometric pressure, and not the barometric pressure corrected to sea level that is normally reported by airport control towers as the altimeter setting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Ambient Conditions”, p. 10-58

notes.front: Before a thrust check, a mechanic reads the air temperature from the terminal roof, 20 m above the runway. What is wrong?
notes.back: D: The engine senses air just above the runway surface, so that temperature is needed
notes.explanation: The engine senses temperature at its compressor inlet, the actual air just above the runway.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; any local reading will do
B) Humidity should be measured instead
C) Temperature should be taken at the tower
D) The engine senses air just above the runway surface, so that temperature is needed
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the engine's sensitivity to inlet temperature. B: the handbook asks for the temperature and pressure the engine senses, not humidity. C is still not the air the engine takes in.
notes.evidence: The engine senses the air temperature and pressure at the compressor inlet. This is the actual air temperature just above the runway surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Ambient Conditions”, p. 10-58

notes.front: After prolonged high-power operation, how should a turbine engine be cooled before shutdown?
notes.back: Run it below a low power setting, preferably at idle, for 5 minutes.
notes.explanation: This prevents possible seizure of the rotors, especially after long high-rpm ground runs such as trimming.
notes.evidence: It is recommended the engine be operated at below a low power setting, preferably at idle for a period of 5 minutes to prevent possible seizure of the rotors. This applies, in particular, to prolonged operation at high rpm on the ground, such as during engine trimming.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Shutdown”, p. 10-58

notes.front: Why can turbine wheels seize after a hot shutdown without cool-down?
notes.back: The case cools faster than the massive wheels and shrinks onto them while they still rotate.
notes.explanation: The case is cooled from inside and outside, but the wheels are not cooled so readily.
notes.evidence: Consequently, the case and the wheels lose their residual heat at different rates after the engine has been shut down. The case, cooling faster, tends to shrink upon the wheels, that are still rotating. Under extreme conditions, the turbine blades may squeal or seize
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Shutdown”, p. 10-59

notes.front: After a hot shutdown the turbine will not turn by hand. What should the mechanic do?
notes.back: D: Leave it until it has cooled enough to free the wheels
notes.explanation: Seizure normally does no harm provided no one tries to turn the engine until it has cooled.
notes.choices:
A) Use a bar to free the wheel at once
B) Motor it with the starter until it frees
C) Reject the turbine assembly
D) Make no attempt to turn it until it has cooled enough to free the wheels
notes.choicesExplained: A and B try to turn the engine before it has cooled. C: no harm normally results if the engine is left to cool.
notes.evidence: Should the turbine wheels seize, no harm normally results, provided no attempt is made to turn the engine over until it has cooled sufficiently to free the wheels.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Engine Shutdown”, p. 10-59

notes.front: An engine shows high exhaust gas temperature, low rpm and high fuel flow at all power settings. What is the probable cause?
notes.back: B: Possible turbine damage and/or loss of turbine efficiency
notes.explanation: The troubleshooting table gives turbine damage or lost turbine efficiency for these symptoms.
notes.choices:
A) An engine pressure ratio indication with a high reading error
B) Possible turbine damage and/or loss of turbine efficiency
C) Low ambient temperature
D) A clogged fuel nozzle filter
notes.choicesExplained: A gives low rpm, exhaust gas temperature and fuel flow, not high temperature and fuel flow. C would not raise exhaust temperature. D is not listed for these symptoms.
notes.evidence: Possible turbine damage and/or loss of turbine efficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting Turbine Engines”, p. 10-60

notes.front: An engine reaches its target pressure ratio for takeoff but with high exhaust gas temperature. What does the table suggest?
notes.back: B: Engine out of trim: check with an analyser and re-trim
notes.explanation: Figure 10-75 lists "engine out of trim" as the probable cause of high exhaust gas temperature at the target engine pressure ratio for takeoff.
notes.choices:
A) Replace the turbine
B) Engine out of trim: check with an analyser and re-trim
C) Clean the compressor
D) Replace the fuel heater
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are actions for other malfunctions in the table.
notes.evidence: Engine out of trim. • Check engine with jetcal. Re-trim as desired.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Troubleshooting Turbine Engines”, p. 10-60

notes.front: What causes most thermodynamic turbine failures?
notes.back: Ice, excess air bleed or leakage, or faulty controls that permit compressor stall or excess fuel.
notes.explanation: These upset the air used to cool combustion temperatures to levels turbine materials can tolerate.
notes.evidence: In general, most thermodynamic failures are caused by ice, excess air bleed or leakage, or faulty controls that permit compressor stall or excess fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Introduction”, p. 9-1

notes.front: What does turboprop engine operation chiefly require attention to?
notes.back: Engine operating limits, the throttle or power lever setting, and the torquemeter pressure gauge.
notes.explanation: Torquemeter pressure is roughly proportional to total power, so it measures engine performance.
notes.evidence: The turboprop chiefly requires attention to engine operating limits, the throttle or power lever setting, and the torquemeter pressure gauge.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Turboprop Operation”, p. 10-59

notes.front: On older aircraft, which part of the power lever control system must be rigged after each engine or fuel control change?
notes.back: The control system from the pylon to the engine.
notes.explanation: The airframe cables and rods to the pylon are usually not disturbed at engine change.
notes.evidence: The control system from the pylon to the engine must be rigged after each engine change and fuel control change.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Rigging Power Controls”, p. 8-14

notes.front: After rigging a fuel control linkage, the rigging pins bind and are hard to pull out. What does this show?
notes.back: A: The cables are not rigged properly and should be rechecked
notes.explanation: Correctly rigged cables let the rigging pins be removed without binding.
notes.choices:
A) The cables are not rigged properly and should be rechecked
B) The rigging is correct; pins are meant to be tight
C) The pins are the wrong size
D) The cable tension is too low only
notes.choicesExplained: B contradicts the source: pins should come out freely. C and D guess at causes the source does not name.
notes.evidence: The pins should be free to be removed without any binding; if they are hard to remove, the cables are not rigged properly and should be rechecked.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Rigging, Inspections, & Adjustments”, p. 8-13

notes.front: Which event requires the engine to be retrimmed?
notes.back: C: Replacing the fuel control unit
notes.explanation: The handbook lists fuel control replacement, low maximum thrust, engine change and excessive throttle stagger.
notes.choices:
A) Replacing a compressor inlet screen
B) Changing the oil
C) Replacing the fuel control unit
D) Washing the engine
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are not among the events that call for retrimming.
notes.evidence: The engine must be retrimmed after a fuel control unit is replaced, the engine does not develop maximum thrust, engine change, or excessive throttle stagger.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Adjusting the Fuel Control”, p. 8-14

notes.front: A mechanic must trim an engine with a light wind blowing from behind the aircraft. What should be done?
notes.back: D: Head the aircraft into the wind before trimming
notes.explanation: Trimming with a tailwind risks reingesting hot exhaust, and accuracy is best into the wind.
notes.choices:
A) Trim now; wind does not matter
B) Add 5 minutes to the stabilisation time
C) Trim at part power only
D) Head the aircraft into the wind before trimming
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that hot exhaust gases may be reingested with a tailwind. C and B do not remove the tailwind.
notes.evidence: Do not trim when there is a tailwind because hot exhaust gases may be reingested. As a practical matter, the engine should never be trimmed when icing conditions exist because of the adverse effects on trimming accuracy.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Adjusting the Fuel Control”, p. 8-14

notes.front: Under what weather condition should an engine never be trimmed?
notes.back: When icing conditions exist.
notes.explanation: Precise, controlled conditions are needed to keep the minimum thrust level aircraft performance is based on.
notes.evidence: Engines should never be trimmed if icing conditions exist.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-41

notes.front: What two readings are taken immediately before trimming, and from them what is computed?
notes.back: Ambient air temperature and field barometric pressure (not sea level); the target turbine discharge pressure or pressure ratio is computed.
notes.explanation: The temperature must match the air actually entering the engine.
notes.evidence: In general, the procedure consists of obtaining the ambient air temperature and the field barometric pressure (not sea level) immediately preceding the trimming of the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-41

notes.front: In a condition monitoring program, what could a shift in key parameters over time warn of?
notes.back: Serious internal deterioration, meaning the engine should be overhauled.
notes.explanation: The program watches trends, not single readings.
notes.evidence: A shift in key parameters (change over time) could be a warning that the engine has serious internal deterioration and should be overhauled.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Turbine Engine Condition Monitoring Programs”, p. 8-2

notes.front: Daily readings show an engine's parameters drifting steadily away from their baseline over weeks, though each is within limits. What does this suggest?
notes.back: C: Possible serious internal deterioration; overhaul may be due
notes.explanation: Condition monitoring looks for trend shifts, which could warn of internal deterioration.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, since each reading is within limits
B) A faulty instrument only
C) Possible serious internal deterioration; overhaul may be due
D) The engine needs retrimming daily
notes.choicesExplained: A misses the point of trend monitoring. B and D are not what a trend shift is said to indicate.
notes.evidence: A shift in key parameters (change over time) could be a warning that the engine has serious internal deterioration and should be overhauled.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Turbine Engine Condition Monitoring Programs”, p. 8-2

notes.front: What is a compressor surge?
notes.back: A stall that affects the entire compressor and seriously restricts the airflow through the engine.
notes.explanation: A stall may involve only one or more blades; a surge involves the whole compressor.
notes.evidence: Compressor surge. A stall that affects the entire compressor and seriously restricts the airflow through the engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), glossary, “Compressor surge”, p. G-7

notes.front: During a rapid acceleration, what can happen if fuel flow increases too rapidly?
notes.back: An over-rich mixture, with the possibility of rich blowout or compressor stall.
notes.explanation: Extra energy must reach the turbine to accelerate, but not faster than the air can support.
notes.evidence: However, if the fuel flow increases too rapidly, an over rich mixture can be produced, with the possibility of a rich blowout or compressor stall.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Engine Fuel System—General Requirements”, p. 2-33

notes.front: During a test, a faulty fuel control lets fuel flow rise far faster than airflow as the power lever is slammed forward. Which problem is most likely?
notes.back: D: Rich blowout or compressor stall
notes.explanation: Excess fuel for the mass airflow can exceed turbine limits or produce compressor stall and rich blowout.
notes.choices:
A) Lean flameout
B) Ram recovery loss
C) Hung start
D) Rich blowout or compressor stall
notes.choicesExplained: A comes from too little fuel. C happens during starting. B is unrelated to fuel scheduling.
notes.evidence: If the quantity of fuel becomes excessive in relation to mass airflow through the engine, the limiting temperature of the turbine blades can be exceeded, or it will produce compressor stall and a condition referred to as rich blowout.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Engine Fuel System—General Requirements”, p. 2-33

notes.front: What are two current uses of compressor bleed air?
notes.back: Any two, among others: cabin pressurisation, heating and cooling; de-icing and anti-icing; pneumatic starting of engines.
notes.explanation: The handbook also lists auxiliary drive units.
notes.evidence: Some of the current applications of bleed air are: 1. Cabin pressurization, heating, and cooling; 2. Deicing and anti-icing equipment; 3. Pneumatic starting of engines; and 4. Auxiliary drive units (ADU).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Compressor Section”, p. 1-38

notes.front: Engine designers need bleed air to cool the turbine bearings. Which compressor stage is it usually bled from?
notes.back: C: A stage with enough pressure where the air is not yet too warm
notes.explanation: Air heats as it is compressed, so cooling air comes from a stage before it gets too warm.
notes.choices:
A) The final stage, where pressure is highest
B) Any stage, since temperature does not matter
C) A stage with enough pressure where the air is not yet too warm
D) The fan duct only
notes.choicesExplained: A gives the hottest air. B ignores that compressed air heats up. D is not what the source describes.
notes.evidence: This bleed air, as it is called, is usually bled off a compressor stage at a point where air has enough pressure but has not yet become too warm (as the air is compressed, it becomes heated).
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 6, “Lubrication”, p. 6-21

notes.front: In gas turbine preservation, what is usually done to the lubrication and fuel systems?
notes.back: Lubrication system: usually drained, perhaps flushed with preservative oil. Fuel system, including the fuel control: generally filled with preservative oil.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer's instructions are always followed.
notes.evidence: The lubrication system is usually drained and may or may not be flushed with preservative oil. The engine fuel system is generally filled with preservative oil, including the fuel control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Preservation & Depreservation of Gas Turbine Engines”, p. 8-22

notes.front: A stored gas turbine engine is being returned to service. What must be done with the preservative oil in its fuel system?
notes.back: A: Flush it completely by motoring the engine and bleeding the fuel system
notes.explanation: Depreservation requires the preservative oil to be completely flushed from the fuel system.
notes.choices:
A) Flush it completely by motoring the engine and bleeding the fuel system
B) Drain the fuel tanks only
C) Leave it; it burns off on start
D) Mix it with fuel for the first flight
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D leave preservative oil in the fuel system.
notes.evidence: Before the engine can be returned to service, the preservative oil must be completely flushed from the fuel system by motoring the engine and bleeding the fuel system.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “Preservation & Depreservation of Gas Turbine Engines”, p. 8-22

notes.front: With which engines is the QECA system most commonly used?
notes.back: Large turbine engines used in the airlines.
notes.explanation: Many QECA procedures also apply to other methods of engine buildup and installation.
notes.evidence: Because the QECA system is most commonly used with large turbine engines used in the airlines, such engines are used to describe QECA buildup and installation procedures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 8, “QECA Buildup Method for Changing of Engines”, p. 8-3

notes.front: A turbine airliner sits at the gate with its main engines off. The crew needs electrical power and bleed air. What supplies them, per the handbook?
notes.back: D: The auxiliary power unit
notes.explanation: An APU provides electrical power and bleed air on the ground, and a backup generator in flight.
notes.choices:
A) The accessory gearbox
B) The quick engine change assembly
C) The free turbine
D) The auxiliary power unit
notes.choicesExplained: A is driven only when the main engine turns. C is part of a turboprop or turboshaft engine. B is an engine change package, not a power source.
notes.evidence: An APU is used on turbine-powered aircraft to provide electrical power and bleed air on the ground and a backup generator in flight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 1, “Types & Construction”, p. 1-37

notes.front: Why must a jetcal analyser be grounded when used on an alternating-current supply?
notes.back: Its wire-wound probes induce a voltage on the case that can shock the operator slightly, noticeably on damp days.
notes.explanation: It is grounded through the pigtail lead in the power inlet cable.
notes.evidence: This condition is not apparent during dry weather, but on damp days the operator can be shocked slightly. Therefore, for the operator's protection, the jetcal analyzer should be grounded using the pigtail lead in the power inlet cable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Analyzer Safety Precautions”, p. 10-61
